analysis.one_liner: Bans bisphenol A in food and beverage containers and forces FDA re-review of food-contact chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate health committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat any food or beverage container containing BPA — the chemical long used in can linings and hard plastic — as adulterating the food inside, effectively banning it 180 days after enactment. Companies that could prove BPA was technologically impossible to replace could get a one-year renewable waiver, but their products would carry a warning label that BPA can leach into food and may harm prenatal and child health. It also bars replacements that are carcinogens, reproductive toxins, or endocrine disruptors, and requires the FDA to periodically re-review chemicals already approved for food contact.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially infants, children, pregnant women, and other groups disproportionately exposed to BPA through canned and packaged food. Workers handling food-contact chemicals and communities with high exposure would also gain from the bill's broader re-review of food-contact substances.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Canned and packaged food consumers, especially infants

how_it_helps.text: Treats containers made with or releasing BPA as adulterating the food inside, banning them for interstate commerce 180 days after enactment, with limited one-year waivers only where replacement is proven technologically infeasible [S3].
Requires any waived product to carry a prominent label warning that BPA can leach into food and may harm prenatal development and the health of children and adults [S3].
Prohibits BPA from being replaced with likely carcinogens, reproductive or developmental toxins, or endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and directs FDA to promote safer alternatives [S3].

Requires FDA to select and re-review already-approved food additives and food-contact substances — including those generally recognized as safe — for low-dose and aggregate-exposure harms to vulnerable populations, and to revoke approvals it can no longer stand behind [S3].

Requires manufacturers to notify FDA before introducing a food-contact substance, including determinations that the substance poses no adverse low-dose effects and no reproductive or developmental toxicity [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Canned food and beverage makers, packaging manufacturers, and chemical suppliers that produce BPA-based can linings, which would need to reformulate products, prove feasibility for waivers, or label canned goods with a health warning within 180 days of enactment. Some costs could be passed to consumers through packaging prices.

drawbacks.text: The 180-day timeline for banning BPA in containers packed with food is short for can supply chains, which historically depended on epoxy linings containing BPA, and waiver applications plus warning labels would add compliance costs that could raise packaged-food prices modestly [S3].

The FDA has maintained in its own reviews that BPA is safe at the low levels currently found in food, so supporters of the status quo would argue the bill bans a substance ahead of the agency's own safety determination — a cost the bill accepts in exchange for precaution on prenatal and childhood exposure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit targets a real, well-studied exposure route: BPA is an endocrine-active chemical that leaches from can linings, and infants and pregnant women are the groups most exposed through canned food. The main costs are reformulation and labeling expenses for the canning and packaging industries, which the bill's waiver and phase-in provisions are designed to soften, and a modest risk of premature bans if the FDA's own low-dose safety findings are correct. On balance the bill trades small, diffuse consumer costs for precautionary protection of a vulnerable population, and the one clear weakness is the tight 180-day timeline.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Ban Poisonous Additives Act of 2016 in the Senate on September 28, 2016 [S1].
On the day of introduction, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which was its final action [S5].
The committee held no hearing, reported no version, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Canned food, beverage, and packaging manufacturers kept operating under existing rules and avoided the cost of replacing BPA linings or labeling products with health warnings; no consumer or health benefit was realized.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and referred it to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: American Chemistry Council
against.role: BPA and plastics industry trade group
against.what_they_did: The main trade association representing BPA producers and users has long opposed legislative bans on BPA, including state and federal proposals like this one; it never needed to lobby this bill directly, which died with no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator signed on besides the sponsor, so the record shows no partisan split — only one Democrat's sponsorship and a silent committee.

industries.note: Cans have historically relied on BPA-based epoxy linings; the bill would force reformulation or a warning label that BPA may harm prenatal development and children's health within 180 days, and waivers would be limited to one-year terms. Industry compliance costs would partly pass through to packaged-food prices.

industries.industry: Food packaging and can-lining chemical suppliers
industries.note: BPA producers and suppliers of BPA-based food-contact substances would lose their largest food-market application, and the bill would add premarket notification duties and periodic safety re-reviews for food-contact chemicals generally.

The bill directs FDA to promote, facilitate, and incentivize safer replacements for BPA, creating demand for BPA-free can linings and containers, and explicitly forbids substitutions that are carcinogens, reproductive toxins, or endocrine disruptors.
